title: Man. Post. Cap. II §XIX: Placeus — no prior convention; theses and Synod letters
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. As to what he says, that I variously played in the name of imputation, I was very far from that, and as much as I could I acted seriously, as became one studious of truth and peace. I also abhorred all tergiversation, and nothing was prior for me than that I should purge the state of the question from every impediment, and make it clear and liquid, lest any place could be for tergiversation or dissimulation or declining. But that he accuses me as if I had not stood by agreements, I cannot wonder enough. For how had we agreed at the beginning of the Dispute, or had it been agreed between us about the signification of the word imputation, who had never disputed between us about that matter? For it was never granted me to see the Learned Man, or to speak with him face to face. And that he would confer with me about this question, I could by no means obtain. But when he says, Now it is gone into all other things, perhaps you think, Reader, that he designates this later manuscript of mine or at least the time when it was written. But it is not so. For the words of mine which he subjoins are not drawn from this Manuscript of mine, but partly from my Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, published five years before this controversy began, partly from the later of the two letters which alone I wrote to him, two or three months after the last National Synod: In the former I was disputing nothing, only asking him modestly in what sense the Synod's Decree on imputation was to be understood, concerning the Mediate, or concerning the Immediate? In the latter truly I briefly showed that neither the reasons brought by me in the theses attack mediate imputation, nor that great Theologians were lacking who denied the immediate while confessing the mediate. For he had written back that both those things were to be shown, which when done by me, for some time he refused to answer me; at last truly, giving me second letters, he protested that he would not answer me about that matter, nor dispute with me or with any other about that business, except in the next National Synod. And so we made an end of writing letters back and forth.
pass_b_english: Placeus: He says I played variously with the name of imputation. I was nowhere near that. I treated the matter as seriously as I could, as one who cares for truth and peace. I also shrank from every evasion. My first aim was to clear the state of the question of every obstacle and make it plain and liquid, so that there would be no room left for tergiversation, dissimulation, or side-stepping. That he charges me with breaking agreements I can scarcely believe. How had we 'agreed' at the opening of the Dispute, or settled between us the sense of the word imputation, when we had never disputed that point with each other? I was never allowed even to see the learned man or speak with him face to face, and I could by no means get him to confer with me on this question. When he says 'Now everything is shifted,' you may think, Reader, that he means this later manuscript of mine, or at least the time when it was written. Not so. The words of mine he quotes are not taken from this Manuscript, but partly from my Theses on the state of fallen man before grace—published five years before this controversy began—and partly from the later of the only two letters I wrote him, two or three months after the last National Synod. In the first letter I disputed nothing; I only asked him modestly how the Synod's Decree on imputation was to be understood—of the Mediate, or of the Immediate? In the second I briefly showed that the reasons I had given in the theses do not attack mediate imputation, and that great theologians have not been lacking who deny the immediate while confessing the mediate. He had written back that both points must be shown; when I had done so, he for some time refused to answer; at last, in a second letter, he protested that he would not answer me on the matter, nor dispute it with me or with anyone else, except in the next National Synod. And so we ended writing letters to each other.
source_text: PLAC. Quod ait me, in nomine imputationis varie lusisse, ab eo longissime abfui, & quam maxime potui serio egi, ut veritatis & pacis decebat studiosum. Abhorrui etiam ab omni tergiversatione, & nihil mihi prius fuit quam ut statum quaestionis purgarem ab omni impedimento, & clarum facerem & liquidum, ne ullus vel tergiversationi, vel dissimulationi, vel declinationi locus esse posset. Quod autem me accusat, quasi conventis non steterim, satis mirari nequeo. Quomodo enim consenseramus Disputationis initio, aut convenerat inter nos de vocis imputationis significatu, qui nunquam ea de re inter nos disputaveramus? Virum enim Doctum mihi nunquam datum est, videre, aut coram alloqui. Ut autem de hac quaestione mecum conferre vellet, impetrare nulla ratione potui. Cum autem dicit, Nunc in alia omnia itur, putas fortasse, Lector, eum hoc meum manufcriptum posterius aut saltem tempus quo scriptum est, designare. At non ita est. Quae enim subjungit verba mea non petuntur ex hoc meo Manufcripto, sed partim ex Thesibus meis de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam, quinquennio, antequam inciperet ista controversia, publicatis, partim ex duarum epistolarum quas solas ad eum scripsi, posteriore, duobus aut tribus a Synodo postrema Nationali mensibus: In priore autem nihil disputabam, tantum ex ipso quaerebam modeste, qua de imputatione Decretum Synodi esset intelligendum, de Mediata, an de Immediata? In posteriore vero breviter ostendebam, nec rationes a me in thesibus allatas mediatam oppugnare imputationem, nec defuisse magnos Theologos qui immediatam negarent confessa mediata. Illud enim utrumque rescripserat ostendendum esse, quod ubi a me factum est, aliquamdiu respondere mihi renuit; tandem vero datis ad me secundis literis protestatus est se mihi ea de re non responsurum, neque mecum aut cum alio ullo eo de negotio disputaturum, nisi in proxima Synodo Nationali. Atque ita finem scribendarum invicem literarum fecimus.
